name: Victor Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work with my uncle Karl at Oakley Farm. A hundred and twenty suckler cows, that's cows that raise their own calves for beef, and about sixty hectares we cut for hay. Winter mornings it's feeding round the sheds, bedding, checking the cows due to calve. Summer is all hay: mowing, turning, baling, and getting it in before the rain. We sell small bales to horse owners, they're loyal customers. What I like is calving, honestly, when it goes right. What wears me out is haymaking when the forecast lies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I use one to check what cattle are fetching at different markets before we sell, and once to write an advert for the bales. It's handy. I'm not going to go mad with it. I'm engaged to Hanna, she works at the bank in town, and we're getting married next August. We've got about four months saved, though the wedding's eating into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the world I'd bet on, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Cows still need feeding, hay still needs baling. A computer helps with prices, that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be pleased. It leaves room for what I actually want, which is to take on more of the farm from Karl and maybe buy a bit of land of my own one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Use the price checker more, maybe let it plan the hay cutting around the forecast if the neighbours say it works. Get married, keep saving, look at renting a few more fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would renting more fields take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eight thousand a year for twenty hectares round here. We'd need the bank to like us, which Hanna says is her department. It'd mean more hay to sell and more summer grazing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest worry in this picture, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feed and fuel prices, and government rules on cattle. Every year there's a new form about where a calf's been. Let farmers farm, that's all I ask.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because cows still need feeding and hay still needs baling. A computer helps with prices and that's about it.
S0.think: Privately he'd be pleased, because it leaves room to take on more of his uncle's farm. One day he'd like to buy land of his own.
S0.do: Carries on with the herd and haymaking, using the price checker more and perhaps forecast-based hay planning once neighbours prove it. Marries, keeps saving and looks at renting about twenty more hectares.
S0.quote: Let farmers farm, that's all I ask.
S0.fieldNote: Victor is ambitious in a quiet, practical way: more land, his own one day. His complaints are about costs and paperwork, not technology. He adopts tools only once neighbours have shown they work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. I think that's the one we're actually heading for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good farmers will adapt like they always have. Tractors replaced horses, didn't they. I'd say it at the market, and I'd say don't wait for the government to hold your hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it helps us more than hurts. Beef and hay are hard to fully automate, there's a lot of judgement. But the beef price might drop if big feedlots get cheaper, and that'd squeeze us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for a couple of farms nearby to try things, then copy what works: cow collars that track heat and health, maybe a robot that pushes feed up in the shed. That's money, a few thousand. I'd use AI more for selling and planning. And I'd keep the horse-hay customers close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, bit. More focused than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you trust a neighbour's experience over a salesman's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the neighbour's paying for it with his own money. When Mr Davies bought a bale wrapper, I went and watched it for a whole afternoon before Karl bought one. That's how it works round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Karl take the cow collars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, then he'd love them. That's Karl. He said the same about the mobile phone.

S1.say: I'd say good farmers will adapt like they always have, as tractors replaced horses. He'd tell people at the market not to wait for the government to hold their hand.
S1.think: Privately he thinks it helps more than hurts, since beef and hay need lots of judgement. His worry is a lower beef price if large feedlots get cheaper.
S1.do: Waits for nearby farms to try new kit, then copies what works, such as cow health collars and a feed-pushing robot costing a few thousand. Uses AI more for selling and keeps hay customers close.
S1.feel: Slightly uneasy but more focused than worried.
S1.quote: When Mr Davies bought a bale wrapper, I went and watched it for a whole afternoon before Karl bought one.
S1.fieldNote: His trust runs through neighbours who've spent their own money, not salesmen or governments. He frames change as normal farming history. His concern is market price, not his own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. The wedding's in nine months. So, a year and a bit after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep your head and look after your own. Family first. I wouldn't be calling for handouts, I'd be telling people to get together and help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's frightening. If robots can calve a cow and bale hay, a big company can run a beef farm with nobody. Our beef would be worth less than it costs. Karl's sixty-two, he might just sell, and then I've got nothing to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married, but I'd make the wedding smaller, cut it from a hundred and twenty guests to forty, and put the difference in savings. I'd talk to Karl about the farm's future straight away. And I'd keep the horse-hay trade going, because horse people want a person they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sort of tight in the chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hanna say about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be disappointed, then she'd say it's sensible, because she's the sensible one. Her mum would be the one who's upset. I'd have to take her mum out for lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to see what works for others before I jump. That's how I do things, I watch first. Two years, I'd be guessing, and guessing with a new wife and no farm.

S2.say: I'd say keep your head and look after your own, with family first. He wouldn't call for handouts but would tell people to band together and help each other.
S2.think: Privately he finds it frightening, since a company could run a beef farm with nobody and push prices below cost. His uncle might simply sell, leaving him nothing to take over.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding from 120 guests to 40 and puts the difference into savings. Talks with his uncle about the farm's future at once and protects the direct hay trade with horse owners.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight feeling in his chest.
S2.quote: Two years, I'd be guessing, and guessing with a new wife and no farm.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline threatens his biggest plan, inheriting a farm, rather than a job. He stays firmly against handouts and turns to family and neighbours. The wedding shrinks but goes ahead, which says a lot about his priorities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's enough to make some moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers should get ready the way they always have: work hard, get smart, and don't wait to be rescued. I'd probably say some of that on the farmers' forum online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to change the kind of beef we sell. Direct to customers, freezer boxes, the farm's name on it. If big robot farms make cheap beef, I'd make the kind people pay more for because they know where it's from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start selling beef boxes direct, maybe ten a month, using AI for the website and orders once I'd seen others do it. Year two, a small cold room, around six thousand. Get married, keep the hay going. And I'd have the hard talk with Karl about passing the farm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But I'd feel like I was steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take on a cold room in a picture where farming is under threat. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But a cold room you can sell, and a customer list is worth more than a tractor. I'd rather owe a bit on something that sells direct than sit tight and lose everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the hard talk with Karl sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Karl, if you're going to sell, tell me now, not in year four. And if you're not, let's write down how I take over. He'd go quiet, then he'd put the kettle on. That's how you know he's thinking.

S3.say: I'd say farmers should get ready as they always have: work hard, get smart and don't wait to be rescued. He might post some of that on an online farmers' forum.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years is enough to switch to selling beef direct under the farm's name. If robot farms make cheap beef, he'd sell the kind people pay more for.
S3.do: Starts selling about ten beef boxes a month direct, using AI for the website and orders once others have shown it works. Adds a small cold room in year two for around six thousand and plans the farm handover with his uncle.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but feeling like he's steering.
S3.quote: A customer list is worth more than a tractor.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he goes from defence to building a direct beef business. He accepts debt for something he can sell, which fits his free-market outlook. Settling the farm's succession matters to him as much as the business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Probably a dad by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Learn, plan, build. I'd be careful not to sound like I'm telling anyone else how to live, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd come out of it with a smaller farm that sells straight to people, and a few robots doing the heavy lifting. That's not a bad life. The worry is whether people still have money to buy good beef if nobody's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the beef box trade slowly over the first few years. I'd buy kit once it was proven and cheaper, maybe year five or six. I'd talk to Karl about taking over properly by year four. Hanna and I would start a family, and I'd want to buy the house rather than rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry about who's buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's an interesting worry, who's buying. Say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots do all the work, who's got wages? My beef boxes need people with jobs. I don't know the answer. I'm not keen on handouts, but somebody has to have money to spend or nothing works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm guessing and scared. Ten years, I watch, copy what works, and build. Ten years is how farming's always done things, slowly. I'd be fine.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work: learn, plan, build. He'd be careful not to sound like he was telling others how to live.
S4.think: Privately he expects a smaller farm selling direct with robots doing the heavy work, which wouldn't be a bad life. He worries whether people will have money for good beef if few are working.
S4.do: Builds the beef box trade slowly and buys machinery once it's proven and cheaper, around year five or six. Arranges to take over the farm by year four, starts a family and aims to buy a house.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry about who will be buying.
S4.quote: I'm not keen on handouts, but somebody has to have money to spend or nothing works.
S4.fieldNote: He sees the slow picture as matching how farming has always changed. His worry about customers losing wages pulls against his dislike of handouts, and he admits the tension. Family and home buying feature strongly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The wedding, Karl maybe selling, no time to watch what works. What would help is clear rules so families can pass farms on without a huge tax bill, and less paperwork so small farms can sell meat direct without jumping through hoops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Everyone worries about the farmers, but if nobody's earning, nobody's buying my beef. I'd want someone cleverer than me working on that.

headlineQuote: A customer list is worth more than a tractor.
portrait: Victor Weber is a 27-year-old who runs a 120-cow suckler beef herd and a small hay business with his uncle Karl, hoping to take the farm over one day. He's engaged to Hanna, who works at a bank, with a wedding planned for next August and about four months saved. He's traditional and free-market, dislikes handouts and trusts neighbours who've tested kit with their own money. In the fast AGI picture his fear is losing the farm he expects to inherit; with more time he plans beef boxes sold direct and a proper handover. He admits a nagging worry about who will buy good beef if nobody earns wages.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it could cost him the farm he hopes to take over just as he's getting married, with no time to watch what works.
whatWouldHelp: Clear rules letting families pass on farms without a huge tax bill, and less paperwork for small farms selling meat direct.
